{"rule": "Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and a new passage of about 250 words in the text field.", "text": "The mill at Hollins Beck stopped grinding the winter Tomas turned sixty, and the letter from the co-operative arrived the same week to say the flour would come now by lorry from a plant in the city, sacked and stamped by men who had never heard the wheel turn. Tomas read it in the stone room with the millstones still beside him, then greased the axle out of habit, though nothing would ask it to move.

He still went down to the race at first light. There was nothing to grind, but his ear knew the pitch of water over the sluice better than it knew silence, and the beck did not seem to have heard that the miller had been let go. He would stand on the footbridge as the frost lifted off the meadow, and the farm carts would pass on the lane with their loads turned toward town, and he would count them by the way his father had taught him to count the strokes of the wheel.

The carters said the city flour never soured and never ran short. He believed them. He still watched the wagons rattle back empty of an afternoon, naming each by the lean of its driver, and once the Pryce girl waved from the box seat, which was either habit or kindness, and Tomas did not turn away.

What surprised him was how the bread kept coming to the tables without anyone to grind for it. He had thought himself the wheel. Now he understood he had mostly been the one who listened to it. The valley had never needed his hand on the hopper; it had needed someone on the bridge to believe each morning that the listening mattered.

He went down to the race again the next dawn."}
